title: No best move, one stable pair
hook: Neither player has a move that wins against everything. Can we still predict the game?

knows: dominant strategies: a move that is best whatever the other player does
how to read a payoff table
doesNotKnow: that even when no move is best against everything, a pair of moves where each is a best reply to the other can still pin down the outcome

misconception: Without a move that is best whatever the other does, game theory cannot predict anything.
objective: The learner can check a cell of a payoff table for best replies on both sides, find that (M, L) is the only cell of the stage's game where neither player wants to switch, and name it a (pure) Nash equilibrium.

claims.text: In the stage's game neither player has a move that is best against every reply of the other.
claims.source: Payoffs (row, column), columns L C R: U (3,1)(0,3)(2,0); M (4,2)(1,0)(0,1); D (2,0)(2,1)(1,3). Row's best reply is M against L, D against C, U against R; Column's best reply is C against U, L against M, R against D. Builder's node check: no row or column move weakly dominates the others (scratchpad ncm-e01-checks/check.mjs). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node (scratchpad fc22/nash.mjs): Row's best replies M|L, D|C, U|R; Column's C|U, L|M, R|D, all unique; no move of either player is a best reply to all three of the other's moves.

claims.text: (M, L) is the only cell where each player's move is a best reply to the other's: Row's 4 is the best in column L and Column's 2 is the best in row M; in every other cell someone gains by switching.
claims.source: Builder's node enumeration of all 9 cells: the only pure-strategy cell with both best replies is (M, L). Mixed strategies are not considered and the lesson says 'pure'. Demo.tsx STABLE computes the same. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own enumeration of 9 cells: only (M, L) has both best replies (Row 4 best in L; Column 2 best in M). Each of the 8 others has a strict gain for at least one player. Pure strategies only, as stated.

claims.text: Each cell's message (who switches, to what, and the payoffs compared) follows from the table.
claims.source: Demo.tsx verdict(): compares the cell's payoff with the column's best row payoff and the row's best column payoff from the table in c1. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own messages for all 8 unstable cells match verdict() logic in Demo.tsx (e.g. UL: Row->M 4>3, Col->C 3>1; DR: Row->U 2>1).

claims.text: A pair of moves that are best replies to each other is a Nash equilibrium.
claims.source: Definition. J. F. Nash, 'Equilibrium points in n-person games', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 36(1), 48-49 (1950); E&K ch. 6 (section unconfirmed). Citation from memory; fact-checker confirms. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Definition (pure-strategy case of Nash's equilibrium point). Nash, PNAS 36(1):48-49 (1950) confirmed as bibliographic data via web-search snippets (PMC1063129 record); paper NOT opened (hosts blocked). claims.text: The payoffs are invented and the game is played once.
claims.source: Modelling choice stated on the card and in the reveal. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Convention, present on stage: chip "Payoffs: (Row, Column) · invented"; reveal "Invented payoffs, one round."

recall.question: In a game where no player has a move that is best whatever the other does, which outcome is stable?
options: None: without a best move nothing can be predicted
One where each player's move is the best reply to the other's
The one with the highest total payoff
recall.why: If each move is a best reply to the other, neither player gains by switching alone: a Nash equilibrium, which can exist without any dominant move.
